cargo: The market has been quiet but steady during June, and while a moderate amount of business has been transacted, there is a want of inquiry, the prices remain generally unchanged. The annexed tables show that upon the whole the imports have been moderate and the deliveries fair, but the present stocks are equal to an increased demand. During the past half year the tonnage launched on the Clyde district amounts to about 121,000 tons, being a falling off of about 60,000 tons when compared with the same time last year. About 30,000 tons of new work was secured last month, but the bulk being cargo steamers, the wood trade is not greatly benefited. The rates of wood freights have slightly improved, which adds somewhat to c.i.f. quotations, and should help stocks on hand. The Bank of England rates has receded from 4 per cent. a month ago to 2½ per cent., against 2 per cent. in 1892, 2½ per cent. in 1891, and 4 per cent. in 1890.

raw_line: ONE of the most interesting exhibits on the show-ground at Aberdeen recently was to be found on Stand No. 50. There Messrs. Reid & Leys had a new oil engine brought out by Messrs. Crossley Brothers, Limited, Openshaw, Manchester, the well-known makers of the "Crossley" Otto gas engine. Messrs. Crossley have built this engine on the general lines of their gas engine. It is of 4 horse-power nom., indicating 8 1/2 horse-power, and giving 6 1/2 actual or brake horse-power. In the sole of the engine there is a tank capable of holding 10 gallons of oil. From this tank the oil is pumped up into the vaporiser and another small tank for supplying a lamp, the function of which is to keep the vaporiser and ignition tube hot. The oil on coming into the vaporiser is converted into gas, which passes into the cylinder. It is there mixed with a certain proportion of air, then compressed by the piston, and fired by the ignition tube. The great feature of the engine is its simplicity and cheapness of working. It can be driven for a consumption of oil equal to three-quarters of a pint per brake per hour. The consumption of the oil is controlled by a patent inertia governor, which regulates the consumption according to the actual power being taken out of the engine. In working a full load with oil costing 6d. a gallon, the expense would be between 3d. and 4d. per hour. The cost of oil for carrying oil, as compared with coal, is about 1 to 16, so there is no doubt, considering all these advantages, that this is the motive power for a farm-steading or any place where ordinary coal gas is not available. Mr. John T. Clark, 46, Rose Street, Aberdeen, coachmaker to the Queen, showed a selection of carriages, in which several new features were introduced. Mr. Clark's exhibits have been features of the show for successive years, and his display on this occasion was fully up to his former high standard. Messrs. David Gray & Son, Holburn Street, Aberdeen, at their stand exhibited a variety of carts, wheels, and axles, which were well worthy of the attention of farmers. Messrs. R. & J. Shinnie, Union Row, Aberdeen, the well-known carriage builders, had a collection of machines of superior manufacture. The stand was a covered one, occupied a prominent position in the implement yard; and, as in former years at the Royal Northern Show, the collection of county gentlemen and agriculturalists' vehicles attracted the attention of tourists. The firm exhibited the most recent specimens of their manufacture, including a number of patent improvements; and, alike in design and workmanship, they more than maintained their previous wide reputation.

origin_port: In obtaining trees it is always preferable to purchase them from a local nurseryman, even though a higher price be paid for them, as on account of the short interval the roots have been exposed to the air to a minimum, and when they are finally put into their places there is every chance of success in transplanting. When the trees are taken up, the roots should be carefully covered up with litter or some other suitable material. It is also advisable to preserve a good bunch of fibrous roots in preference to one or two tap roots, as it is from the small, thready
cargo: looking roots that the tree derives its nourishment, and if these are destroyed it is likely to suffer the consequences.

Bullock, Official Receiver, applied for the direction of the Court as to the distribution of the estate of this debtor, who had been twice adjudged bankrupt. cargo: Mr. Bullock explained that the bankrupt formerly carried on business as a builder and contractor in Hanley. On the 4th May, 1884, a receiving order was made against him, and he was adjudged bankrupt. The assets realised were not sufficient to pay the costs, and consequently no dividend was paid to the creditors, and a balance of £50 remained due to the trustee when he obtained his release in September, 1887. After his bankruptcy, he commenced jobbing work in a small way, and his business increasing, he commenced about four or five years ago to take contracts for new buildings. It was not known whether the trustee, prior to obtaining his release, was aware of the bankrupt having commenced to trade again but the Official Receiver, in whom, on the trustee's release, any future assets would rest, was altogether ignorant of the fact. On the 11th May last the bankrupt executed a deed of assignment, and on the 11th July he was again adjudged bankrupt upon a creditor's petition. No trustee had been appointed, and the estate was being realised by the Official Receiver. It was estimated that after paying the costs of the bankruptcy and preferential claims, about £580 would remain for distribution amongst the creditors. It had been arranged that the Official Receiver should apply for the directions of the Court as to the whether (1) the creditors in the first bankruptcy ; (2) the creditors in the second bankruptcy ; or (3) the creditors in both bankruptcies were to be paid.

cargo: Ash. The adjourned public examination of this debtor took place on Monday last at the Aberdare County Court. The debtor, in reply to questions put by the Official Receiver, said that he had paid away a sum of money to cover the charges of the solicitor and the auctioneer in the sale of some property, the mortgagee having sold the property. The debtor was then questioned at considerable length with respect to his transactions with a Mr. Phillips, a solicitor's clerk, from which it appeared that the debtor had received several sums of money on houses he had built from Mr. Phillips. The money was advanced as the houses progressed, and there was no special arrangement as to interest. Mr. Phillips here stated that in the district it was the practice to charge the full amount of interest on progressive mortgages from the date of the first instalment. The Registrar and the Official Receiver both repudiated that statement. The debtor, in the course of further examination, said other persons who had advanced him money had adopted the same practice. The examination was eventually adjourned in order that the debtor might be enabled to file particulars of the mortgages he had received and how they were paid, and the amount of interest paid on each mortgage.
